questions.q: The wave equation relates the speed of a periodic wave to its wavelength and frequency. Which statement correctly gives that relationship?
options: The speed equals the frequency divided by the wavelength
The speed of a periodic wave equals its frequency multiplied by its wavelength, v = fλ
The speed equals the wavelength divided by the frequency
The speed equals the amplitude multiplied by the frequency
questions.explanation: The wave equation is v = fλ: the speed of a periodic wave is its frequency times its wavelength. Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, so v = λ/T as well. Amplitude does not affect wave speed.

questions.q: What is the speed of a sound wave if it has a period of 2.0 ms and a wavelength of 68 cm?
working: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, so use \(v = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}\) (since \(f = \tfrac{1}{T}\))
questions.explanation: The displacement-time graph gives the period, so f = 1/T, and the wave equation v = fλ (here v = λ/T) delivers the speed. Convert milliseconds to seconds and centimetres to metres first.

questions.q: Snell's Law states n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r). A ray of light strikes a glass block of refractive index 1.45 at an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of refraction in the glass?
questions.explanation: By Snell's Law, 1.0 × sin 30° = 1.45 × sin θ, so sin θ = 0.3448 and θ ≈ 20°. The ray bends towards the normal because it enters a medium with a higher refractive index.

questions.q: For total internal reflection to occur at a boundary, which condition on the refractive indices and the incident angle must be met?
options: The light must pass from a lower to a higher refractive index, n1 < n2
The relative refractive index must be less than 1 (n1 > n2) and the incident angle must exceed the critical angle, so all the light is reflected back with no refracted ray
The incident angle must be smaller than the critical angle
The two media must have equal refractive indices
questions.explanation: A critical angle only exists when n1 > n2 (denser to less dense). At incident angles greater than the critical angle, all the light is reflected back into the original medium and no refracted ray is formed — total internal reflection, as used in optical fibres.

questions.q: The energy Q transferred to a substance to change its temperature is given by Q = mcΔT. On what three factors does this transferred energy depend?
options: The mass, the change in temperature, and the specific heat capacity of the substance
The mass, the latent heat, and the change of state
The volume, the pressure, and the temperature
The thermal conductivity, the area, and the thickness
questions.explanation: Q = mcΔT: the energy transferred to change a substance's temperature is directly proportional to its mass m, its change in temperature ΔT, and its specific heat capacity c. Latent heat (Q = mL) instead governs a change of state at constant temperature.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to heat 8.0 kg of water from a room temperature of 15 °C to 85 °C? Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: A temperature change with no change of state, so use Q = mcΔT. The change in temperature is the same number in K or °C (70). The result is about 2400 kJ.

questions.q: From memory: state what Q = mL calculates, and explain why during a change of state the temperature is not increasing even though energy is transferred to the substance.
keyPoints: Q = mL is the energy required to change the state of a substance without a change in temperature, where L is the specific latent heat of fusion or vaporisation.
During the change of state the energy transferred is not increasing the random translational kinetic energy of the particles.
Instead that energy goes into breaking the bonds between particles, so the temperature holds constant while the state changes.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that Q = mL covers a change of state at constant temperature, and that the energy breaks bonds rather than raising particle kinetic energy, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory, explain how a standing wave forms on a guitar string: the incident pulses reach the fixed end, are reflected back inverted with the same wavelength and speed, and where the incident and reflected waves coincide interference between the waves occurs.
keyPoints: The reflected pulses have the same wavelength and speed as the incident pulses but are inverted.
Where the incident waves and the reflected waves coincide, interference between the waves occurs.

At particular frequencies the points of constructive and destructive interference are evenly spaced, so the resultant superimposed wave appears fixed in position — a standing wave with nodes and antinodes.
questions.explanation: When the incident and reflected waves interfere constructively and destructively at evenly spaced positions along the string, the resultant superimposed wave appears fixed in position — a standing wave with nodes and antinodes.

questions.q: When a sound source moves towards a stationary observer (the Doppler effect), what does the observer hear, and does the source's emitted frequency change?
options: A lower frequency, because the emitted frequency itself decreases
A higher effective frequency, while the source keeps emitting the same frequency — only the observed frequency rises
The same frequency, because motion does not affect sound
A higher frequency only if the source also gets louder
questions.explanation: The effective frequency is always heard as higher when the sound source approaches the observer (and lower as it moves away). The source still emits its own constant frequency; the source's motion compresses the wavefronts, shortening the effective wavelength and raising the observed frequency f'.

questions.q: Heat is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation. Which single description correctly matches conduction?
options: The bulk movement of a heated fluid, with warm less-dense fluid rising
The transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves, needing no medium
The transfer of heat through a substance by collisions between neighbouring vibrating particles, with no net movement of particles
The transfer of heat only through a vacuum
questions.explanation: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a substance as a result of collisions between neighbouring vibrating particles; kinetic energy passes from particle to particle with no net movement of particles. Convection is bulk fluid movement; radiation alone needs no medium and can cross a vacuum.

questions.q: Explain the difference between heat and temperature, then explain why a coastal town has a milder climate than an inland desert at the same latitude. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance, whereas heat is energy transferred from a hotter object to a colder one because of the temperature difference between them — energy in transit. A coastal town has a milder climate because water has a very high specific heat capacity: the ocean can absorb and release a large amount of thermal energy with only a small change in its own temperature, so it warms slowly by day and in summer and cools slowly by night and in winter, moderating the temperature of nearby land. An inland desert, lacking this large body of water, heats and cools rapidly, giving temperature extremes.

criteria.descriptor: Defines temperature as the average kinetic energy of particles.
Defines heat as energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
Links water's high specific heat capacity to the ocean buffering temperature change.
Concludes the coast is milder while the inland desert has extremes.

questions.explanation: This connects the heat-versus-temperature distinction to a specific-heat-capacity application, exactly as the episode worked it.
